source.title: The Effect of Label Noise on the Information Content of Neural Representations
source.authors: Ali Hussaini Umar; Franky Kevin Nando Tezoh; Jean Barbier; Santiago Acevedo; Alessandro Laio

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation.
record.tranche_reason: Tests how label noise relates to generalization error using a representation analysis, rather than reproducing the original random-label fitting experiment.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own generalization-error results across label-noise levels. Its statements that networks can interpolate random labels and that noisy labels amplify double descent cite prior work; those cited results are not rows. Training error is not reported.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own test-error measurements after SGD training with fixed random label corruption, directly testing the test-error component of V4. Its representation analysis does not itself test the listed versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate, but representation robustness should be restricted to moderate label noise and strong overparameterization. The authors find that information imbalance mirrors double descent, that noise increases information loss between hidden and pre-softmax representations, and that smaller such loss correlates with better performance. Completely random-label representations can instead be less informative than random features.
record.recipe_differences: Uses FCNN/CNN width sweeps with varying label noise and measures generalization error alongside information imbalance; it does not reproduce the original random-label fitting experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relationship varies with network width and dataset: in the underparameterized regime noise reduces MNIST error and does not significantly affect CIFAR-10 error; higher noise raises the double-descent peak.

fits_no_version.finding: Hidden representations under moderate label noise become approximately equivalent to clean-label representations at strong overparameterization, while noise increases information loss before the output.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Moderate label noise can preserve hidden representation information while degrading output representations.

fits_no_version.finding: Representations trained with completely random labels can be less informative than random features and yield worse accuracy when a classifier is subsequently trained on clean labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training on random labels can impair representation quality relative to untrained random features.

record.problems: Only two baseline vision architectures and datasets are studied. Generalization-error values are presented in figures without numerical values in the text; no uncertainty estimates are stated. Training error is not reported.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results omitted. Figure 5 reports test accuracy for a classifier trained on the clean task using RF, CLEAN and NOISE representations; this does not measure the claim's training or test error for networks trained on random labels.

untested.parts: No own training-error measurements establish interpolation of completely random labels, accompanying chance test error, or unchanged training hyperparameters.
Training-time ratios and convergence speed across corruption fractions are not measured.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs is not tested.
Perfect training fit across corruption fractions, steady degradation through complete corruption to chance, and simultaneous fitting of signal and noise are not established.
Effects of weight decay, dropout, augmentation, and their removal on fitting and generalization are not tested.
No training trajectory measures whether shared real patterns are learned before noisy labels. Endpoint representation differences do not establish learning order.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text contains figure captions but no readable plotted values. Qualitative row states follow the authors' explicit descriptions. The study is not an original source. Missing evidence for untested clauses does not itself justify a limits_scope verdict.

versions.untested_parts: The paper discusses random-label interpolation as prior work but does not report its own training error or test error for a network trained on completely random labels.
Training time and convergence speed across label-noise levels are not reported.
Shuffled-pixel, permuted-pixel and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.
Whether training error remains perfect across noise levels is not reported. The text does not establish that test error rises steadily all the way to chance.
Weight decay, dropout and data augmentation are not tested.
The paper does not measure the order in which networks learn real patterns and noisy labels; the relevant statement cites prior work.
